newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WMC sees 96/97 net in line with forecasts.
newsitem.headline: WMC sees 96/97 net in line with forecasts.

text.p: WMC Ltd said on Thursday that it expected its 1996/97 net profit to be in line with most market forecasts.
"Those brokers that track us well are in line with what we're expecting," WMC manging director Hugh Morgan told an analysts' meeting.
But he gave no figures for the expected results for the year ending June 30.
Morgan also said that real prices for its products were declining at a rate of one to two percent a year.
WMC reported a net profit of A$386.2 million for the year ended June 30, 1996.

Due to expansion under way, including that of the Olympic copper-uranium project and gold and other exploration activities, Morgan said he expected the company's debt to equity ratio to exceed 30 percent temporarily.
"We'll probably get well into the 30s," he said.
Morgan said he expected global demand for copper to remain healthy based in large part on expectations of stronger consumption in Asia as per capita incomes increase.
Alumina prices have shown little change in the past year with spot terms hovering around US$215-225 a tonne but nickel prices have proved to be somewhat of a disappointment, Morgan said.
"Nickel prices were a hell of lot less than we hoped for," he said.
Nickel, gold and copper and, to a lesser extent phosphates, were offering WMC its most meaningful returns, he said.
Turning to production, he said the group's nickel, gold and copper production in 1997/98 would be roughly in line with 1996/97.
The entire Aluminum Co of America -WMC alumina business was operating at full capacity apart from at St Croix in the West Indies, Morgan said.

In a comment on productivity, he noted nickel production at the Kambalda smelter has risen to about 36,000 tonnes a year with a workforce of 650 people from 32,000 tonnes a year with 1,500 people employed a few years ago.
Of gold, Morgan said that while strong demand from the jewellery sector was helping underpin the market, concern over possible central bank selling was tending to undermine prices.
